text: In June of eighteen sixteen, snow fell in New England. In Europe it rained for weeks, and grain rotted in the fields. People called it the year without a summer. A volcano on the other side of the world is the main suspect. This is History, episode five. What do we actually know, and what is still argued about?

April, eighteen fifteen. Mount Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, erupts. The main blast came around April tenth. It is rated seven on the volcanic explosivity scale, the largest eruption in recorded history, and the sound was heard about two thousand kilometers away. Ash, famine and disease followed on the islands nearby. A commonly cited toll is about seventy one thousand deaths in the region, but the estimates vary, and most of those people died of hunger and disease, not the blast.

Why would an eruption cool the whole planet? The key is not ash, which falls out within weeks. It is sulfur dioxide. Lofted high into the stratosphere, it turns into tiny droplets of sulfuric acid that spread around the world and reflect some sunlight back to space. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica hold a large sulfate spike from these years. There is a complication. Another big eruption, never identified, happened around eighteen oh nine, and the sun was also quiet in this period. So scientists still debate how much of the cold to blame on Tambora alone.

How much cooler did it get? Reconstructions from tree rings, diaries and early thermometers give a range, not one number. Averaged over the Northern Hemisphere, summer eighteen sixteen was roughly half a degree to one degree Celsius colder than normal, depending on the study. Some regions of Europe and North America were colder than that. A degree sounds small. But a late frost or a cold wet summer, in a place where people live on one harvest, can be enough to break a crop.

New England. Newspapers and diaries describe a cold May. Then, on June sixth and seventh, snow fell in parts of New England, upstate New York and Quebec. Frost returned in July, and again in August. Corn, the staple crop, failed in many places. Farmers who had lived there for generations were running short of food and feed for their animals. The nickname Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death is popular, but it is not known to be from that year.

Europe had a different problem: not frost, but rain and cold. Records in France, Switzerland, Germany and the British Isles describe a sodden summer, a late harvest, and a poor one. Grain prices climbed sharply, in some places by double. Hungry crowds rioted over bread, and many people left home to beg. Historian John Post called it the last great subsistence crisis in the Western world. Typhus spread in Ireland. How many died in Europe because of the weather? No reliable total exists, and published figures differ widely.

And in America, people moved. Farmers in northern New England had already been heading west toward Ohio and beyond, along with others from many states. The cold years of eighteen sixteen and seventeen are often said to have pushed more families to go. That fits the records of the time, but how many moved because of the weather, and how many would have moved anyway, is not known. Indiana became a state in December of eighteen sixteen. Illinois followed two years later.

Now to the story everyone remembers. In June eighteen sixteen, near Lake Geneva in Switzerland, the poets Lord Byron and Percy Shelley, with Mary Shelley, her stepsister Claire Clairmont and Byron's doctor, John Polidori, were stuck indoors at a villa called Diodati. Mary Shelley later wrote of a wet, ungenial summer with incessant rain. Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story. Mary began the tale that became Frankenstein. Polidori began a story that led to The Vampyre. In July, Byron wrote a poem called Darkness, about the sun going out. The weather there is documented. That the volcano shaped these particular works is an attractive idea, but it is an interpretation. They might well have written them in a dry summer, too.

text: Some popular claims are more doubtful. One says the first bicycle, Karl Drais's running machine of eighteen seventeen, was invented because horses starved without oats. It is a plausible idea, and some historians repeat it, but it is not firmly proven. So, what is established? Tambora erupted in eighteen fifteen. The summer of eighteen sixteen was unusually cold in the Northern Hemisphere. Harvests failed in parts of Europe and North America. What is debated? The exact size of the cooling, how much is due to Tambora, how many people died, and how much the weather changed the course of events.
